summary: strix's current Scope Guard (internal/guard/guard.go) is a clean deterministic chokepoint, but it only checks scope/risk/category/time — it does NOT enforce the MaxRPS/MaxConcurrent fields already declared in RoE (internal/engagement/roe.go), and tools run as plain in-process Go (built-in portscan) or will shell out with no OS-level confinement, no egress allowlist, no kill-switch, and a plain JSONL audit log that silently drops encoding errors and has no tamper-evidence. The single most important architectural insight from mature/responsible platforms (XBOW, AWS/Anthropic agent sandboxes, iron-proxy) is defense-in-depth: the application-layer Scope Guard must be backstopped by an OS-level enforcement layer so that even a buggy tool, a hallucinating planner, or a compromised shelled-out binary physically cannot reach an out-of-scope host. The highest-leverage additions for strix, in order: (1) a default-deny egress enforcement layer keyed to the engagement scope (recommend iron-proxy, a single Go Apache-2.0 binary doing DNS+SNI+CIDR allowlisting, or a strix-native SNI/DNS proxy for the single-binary goal); (2) enforce rate/concurrency limits in the guard/engine using golang.org/x/time/rate plus golang.org/x/sync/semaphore (already-declared config, trivial win); (3) run every shelled-out tool inside a sandbox — bubblewrap on Linux (recommended default: zero-dependency, namespaces+seccomp), with optional gVisor/runsc for untrusted exploit tooling and Podman rootless containers as the heavier portable option; (4) a real kill-switch (context cancellation wired to SIGINT + a watched abort file + per-engagement deadline) and a dry-run that is already present but should become the default; (5) upgrade the audit log to a SHA-256 hash-chained, append-only, tamper-evident ledger and stop swallowing write errors. Net: keep the deterministic Go Scope Guard as the policy brain, but make scope a thing enforced twice — once in Go, once by the OS network/process boundary — so strix can credibly claim it cannot go out of scope.

recommendations.name: iron-proxy (ironsh/iron-proxy) — default-deny egress firewall
recommendations.why: A MITM egress proxy with a built-in DNS server that sits between a sandboxed workload and the network and BLOCKS every outbound request unless the destination matches an allowlist; also validates the upstream resolved IP against denied CIDRs to close SSRF/DNS-rebinding gaps. This is the exact OS-level backstop strix lacks: derive its allowlist directly from engagement.Scope.InScope (and explicitly deny OutOfScope), so even if the planner or a shelled-out tool tries to hit an out-of-scope host, the connection is refused at the boundary. Tradeoff: MITM TLS termination needs strix to provision a CA into the sandbox (fine for tools strix runs; you mostly need it for the SNI/host check, not body inspection, in a pentest context where you DO want to reach the target's content). For the single-static-binary vision, you may instead embed a strix-native SNI+DNS allowlist proxy (see smartSNI as a ~single-file Go reference) to avoid MITM entirely and filter on the TLS SNI / DNS name only.
recommendations.integration: shell-out / sidecar: run as a single Go binary alongside strix; point the sandboxed tool's resolver + HTTP(S)_PROXY at it. Allowlist generated by strix from the engagement scope. Alternative: port its DNS+SNI allowlist logic into strix as a Go package for a true single binary.
recommendations.maturity: Active 2025 OSS project purpose-built for AI agents/CI/sandboxes; niche but directly on-point. smartSNI/EasySNI exist as simpler Go SNI-proxy references if you build your own.

recommendations.name: bubblewrap (bwrap) — per-tool process sandbox (recommended default)
recommendations.why: Zero-dependency, unprivileged Linux sandbox (the engine behind Flatpak) built from user namespaces, mount namespaces, seccomp and cgroups. It is the right default for confining shelled-out tools (nmap, nuclei, future exploit modules): give each tool a read-only minimal filesystem, no host network except the strix egress proxy's namespace, dropped capabilities, and a seccomp filter. Recommended over firejail because firejail is a setuid-root binary with a history of LPE CVEs and is desktop-app oriented; bubblewrap is a clean building block you wrap programmatically. Tradeoff: bubblewrap is a low-level primitive with no templates, so strix must construct the bwrap argv itself — but that is exactly the deterministic control you want.
recommendations.integration: shell-out: strix builds an argv (bwrap --unshare-all --share-net <into proxy netns> --ro-bind / / --seccomp ... -- <tool>) and exec's the tool through it from Go's os/exec. Detect bwrap at startup; skip sandbox with a loud warning if absent.

recommendations.name: gVisor / runsc — strong isolation for untrusted exploit tooling
recommendations.why: A Google user-space application kernel (written in Go) that intercepts syscalls and re-implements the Linux ABI, giving the strongest practical syscall-level isolation short of a VM; used in production at Google for untrusted code. Reserve this for the highest-risk strix actions (running third-party exploit code, RiskHigh category) where a tool itself may be hostile. It is OCI-compatible (runsc), so it slots in as a Docker/Podman runtime (--runtime=runsc). Tradeoff: measurable performance overhead and some syscall-compatibility gaps, plus heavier to ship than bwrap — so make it opt-in per engagement/risk tier, not the default.
recommendations.integration: shell-out: install as an OCI runtime and launch high-risk tools with `runsc` (or `docker/podman run --runtime=runsc`). strix selects runtime based on action.RiskLevel.

recommendations.name: Podman (rootless) — portable container isolation + per-network egress
recommendations.why: Daemonless, rootless container engine; each container runs in its own user namespace with namespaces/cgroups/SELinux, and Podman creates isolated virtual networks (pasta/slirp4netns) so container traffic is segmented from the host. Good heavier-weight alternative to bwrap when strix wants a reproducible tool image (a 'strix-tools' image bundling nmap/nuclei/etc.) and wants to attach that container only to a network where the only reachable route is the iron-proxy egress firewall. Rootless means a compromised tool does not get host root. Tradeoff: bigger dependency than bwrap and pulls images; best for the 'polished product' distribution rather than minimal air-gapped use.
recommendations.integration: shell-out: `podman run --network strix-egress-only --read-only ... strix-tools <cmd>`. strix manages a dedicated podman network whose egress is constrained to the proxy.
recommendations.maturity: Very mature (Podman 5.x, 2025), rootless is the headline feature.

recommendations.name: golang.org/x/time/rate + golang.org/x/sync/semaphore — enforce MaxRPS/MaxConcurrent
recommendations.why: RoE already declares MaxRPS and MaxConcurrent but the guard/engine ignore them — this is the cheapest, highest-credibility fix. Use a token-bucket rate.Limiter (limiter.Wait(ctx) before each network action) sized to MaxRPS, and a weighted semaphore.NewWeighted(MaxConcurrent) around tool execution in engine.handle. This makes strix a polite scanner (avoids knocking over fragile targets — exactly the responsible-scanning concern nmap's docs raise) and turns declared RoE knobs into enforced behavior. Tradeoff: per-action vs per-target limiting — recommend a map of limiters keyed by target host so one busy host can't starve others.
recommendations.integration: go-lib: import directly; add a Limiter to the Guard or a throttler the engine consults before calling t.Execute. Wire ctx so the kill-switch cancels waiting actions too.
recommendations.maturity: Official Go x/ modules, stable, ubiquitous.

recommendations.name: SHA-256 hash-chained append-only audit ledger (in-house) + optional transparency.dev/Trillian concepts
recommendations.why: strix's audit log is the product's core trust artifact ('prove what was and was not done'), yet today it is plain JSONL, single-writer, and Record() silently swallows json.Encode errors so an action could execute with NO durable record. Upgrade to a tamper-evident chain: each entry stores prevHash and entryHash = SHA256(canonical(time,kind,data,prevHash)); periodically write/print the head hash (and ideally have the client co-sign or store it out-of-band) so any later edit/deletion/reordering is detectable. This is the well-established pattern (hash chains, Merkle anchoring) used by Trillian/transparency.dev and recent agent-audit work. Also: stop ignoring write errors (a failed audit write should fail-closed — abort the action), and consider Ed25519-signing the final report + log head. Tradeoff: a pure hash chain gives tamper-evidence, not tamper-proofing; for stronger guarantees periodically anchor the head hash somewhere the operator cannot quietly rewrite (printed to console, emailed to client, committed to git).
recommendations.license: N/A (stdlib crypto/sha256, crypto/ed25519); Trillian is Apache-2.0 if you ever want full Merkle log
recommendations.integration: go-lib: extend internal/audit.Entry with PrevHash/Hash fields and a running head in Log; use crypto/sha256 + crypto/ed25519 from stdlib. No external service needed for the chain.
recommendations.maturity: Hash-chain pattern is standard; Trillian is mature/Google-backed if you scale up.

pitfalls: Two-layer or it's theater: an application-layer Scope Guard alone cannot guarantee in-scope behavior — a buggy tool, a shelled-out binary, an SSRF in a target redirecting strix, or a hallucinating planner can all originate out-of-scope traffic. Scope must ALSO be enforced at the OS network boundary (egress allowlist/firewall). Until that exists, do not market 'cannot go out of scope.'

DNS rebinding / TOCTOU: the guard resolves/validates a hostname, then the tool re-resolves and connects to a different (out-of-scope) IP. Mitigate by validating the actually-resolved IP at connect time against scope CIDRs (iron-proxy does this) — string-matching the target name is insufficient.

The egress allowlist must be derived from BOTH InScope AND OutOfScope and honor strix's 'out-of-scope always wins' rule; a naive allowlist that only adds InScope CIDRs can still permit an OutOfScope host nested inside an InScope CIDR.
Declared-but-unenforced controls erode trust: RoE.MaxRPS and RoE.MaxConcurrent exist in the schema but nothing enforces them today. Shipping config knobs that do nothing is worse than omitting them.

Audit fail-open: audit.Record() ignores json.Encode errors, so a disk-full or broken pipe means actions run with no record. For a forensic/accountability product the audit write should fail-CLOSED (block/abort the action) or at minimum loudly halt the engagement.

Plain JSONL is trivially editable after the fact (by the operator or an attacker with file access); without a hash chain + externally anchored head, the log cannot prove it wasn't altered — undermining the central value proposition.
firejail's setuid-root design has a recurring LPE CVE history; prefer unprivileged bubblewrap. Don't ship a sandbox that enlarges the host attack surface.

Sandboxing is Linux-centric: bubblewrap/gVisor/nsjail/firejail are Linux-only. strix builds on Windows today (per env) — sandbox + nftables egress must degrade gracefully (and warn loudly) on non-Linux, or strix should document that hardened mode requires Linux.

Kill-switch must cancel in-flight work, not just stop scheduling: wire ctx cancellation (SIGINT + watched abort-file + per-engagement deadline from TimeWindows) through rate-limiter Wait(), semaphore Acquire(), and tool Execute(), and ensure shelled-out child processes are killed (process group / container stop), not orphaned.

Time-window enforcement uses time.Now() at decision time but a long-running tool can run past the window's end; enforce the window as a hard deadline on the action's context too, not just an admission check.
open_questions: Primary OS target for hardened mode: is strix's enforcement host Linux (enabling bubblewrap/gVisor/nftables/iron-proxy netns) or must full scope-enforcement work on the Windows dev machine too? This decides whether OS-level egress is a hard guarantee or a Linux-only 'hardened mode.'

Single-static-binary purity vs. best-of-breed: embed a strix-native SNI/DNS allowlist proxy and bwrap-argv builder (keeps one binary, more code to own) OR depend on external binaries (iron-proxy, bwrap, runsc) detected at runtime (faster to ship, adds install deps)? Recommend: native rate-limit + hash-chain now; detect-and-use external bwrap/iron-proxy with graceful degradation.

TLS interception policy: for HTTP tooling, does strix MITM-terminate egress (full body/credential inspection, needs CA in sandbox) or filter only on DNS name + TLS SNI (no MITM, weaker but simpler and never decrypts target traffic)? SNI/DNS-only is likely the right default for a pentest tool.
Kill-switch trust model: should the engagement head-hash / kill-switch be co-signed or co-held by the CLIENT (true accountability) or is operator-local sufficient for v1?
Per-target vs global rate limiting: enforce MaxRPS globally, per-target-host, or both? Per-host avoids one fragile asset being hammered while still capping total load.

Fail-closed audit: confirm desired behavior when an audit write fails mid-engagement — abort the whole engagement, abort just the action, or buffer and continue? For a compliance artifact, fail-closed is the defensible default.
